scenes.tts: Why should stretching a membrane open a channel at all?
scenes.visual: Title card: Tension Pays for Area. A membrane sheet pulled at its edges by outward arrows; a channel sits in it.
scenes.narration: Why should stretching a membrane open a channel at all?

scenes.tts: Start with the simplest picture that could work. The channel is either closed or open.
scenes.visual: Two icons: a closed channel and an open channel, side by side.
scenes.narration: Start with the simplest picture that could work. The channel is either closed or open.

scenes.tts: The open state takes up more room in the plane of the membrane. Call the extra amount the area gained.
scenes.visual: Seen from above, the open channel's outline is larger than the closed one. The extra ring is labelled ΔA, the area gained.
scenes.narration: The open state takes up more room in the plane of the membrane. Call the extra amount the area gained.

scenes.tts: Membrane tension is an in-plane stretch. It is force per unit length of membrane.
scenes.visual: Arrows pull outward along a membrane edge. Label: tension T = force per length.
scenes.narration: Membrane tension is an in-plane stretch. It is force per unit length of membrane.

scenes.tts: Stretching a membrane does work on anything in it that gets wider. That work is tension times the area gained.
scenes.visual: The channel widens as the sheet is pulled. A small energy packet labelled T × ΔA flows into the channel.
scenes.narration: Stretching a membrane does work on anything in it that gets wider. That work is tension times the area gained.

scenes.tts: So tension lowers the energy of the open state, relative to the closed one.
scenes.visual: An energy diagram: closed and open bars. A tension slider rises, and the open bar sinks.
scenes.narration: So tension lowers the energy of the open state, relative to the closed one.

scenes.tts: Write it out. The energy difference equals the resting preference for closed, minus tension times the area gained.
scenes.visual: The equation assembles term by term: ΔG = ΔG₀ − T × ΔA. Each term is labelled as it appears.
scenes.narration: Write it out. The energy difference equals the resting preference for closed, minus tension times the area gained.

scenes.tts: In a slack membrane, the channel prefers to be closed. As tension rises, that preference shrinks.
scenes.visual: Slider at zero: open bar above closed, gap labelled ΔG₀. Slider rises; the gap narrows.
scenes.narration: In a slack membrane, the channel prefers to be closed. As tension rises, that preference shrinks.

scenes.tts: At one particular tension, the preference disappears. Above it, the open state wins.
scenes.visual: The bars cross at one tension, marked on the slider. Beyond it, the open bar sits lower.
scenes.narration: At one particular tension, the preference disappears. Above it, the open state wins.

scenes.tts: Two channels are each open half the time at the same tension. One gains five square nanometres on opening. The other gains three hundred.
scenes.visual: Two channels labelled 5 nm² and 300 nm². A shared mark on a tension axis: both half open here.
scenes.narration: Two channels are each open half the time at the same tension. One gains five square nanometres on opening. The other gains three hundred.

scenes.tts: Which one goes from mostly closed to mostly open over the narrower range of tension?
scenes.visual: On screen: which one switches over the narrower range of tension?
scenes.narration: Which one goes from mostly closed to mostly open over the narrower range of tension?

scenes.tts: The three hundred channel. Each small rise in tension gives it sixty times the energy advantage.
scenes.visual: Two curves drawn at the same half point: the 300 nm² curve nearly vertical, the 5 nm² curve gentle. Label: 300 ÷ 5 = 60.
scenes.narration: The three hundred channel. Each small rise in tension gives it sixty times the energy advantage.

scenes.tts: So a small change in tension swings it all the way from closed to open.
scenes.visual: The steep curve is traced from bottom to top over a tiny tension step.
scenes.narration: So a small change in tension swings it all the way from closed to open.

scenes.tts: To turn the energy into a curve, use the Boltzmann relation from statistical physics.
scenes.visual: Header: Boltzmann relation. The energy diagram slides aside to make room for a curve.
scenes.narration: To turn the energy into a curve, use the Boltzmann relation from statistical physics.

scenes.tts: For a two-state channel, the ratio of open to closed depends on the energy difference, compared with thermal energy.
scenes.visual: On screen: open/closed = exp(−ΔG/k_B·T_abs). Label: k_B·T_abs, thermal energy, about 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J at room temperature.
scenes.narration: For a two-state channel, the ratio of open to closed depends on the energy difference, compared with thermal energy.

scenes.tts: For a two-state channel at equilibrium, this gives the fraction of channels open. Patch papers fit the same curve to current. That reading assumes current tracks the fraction open. The curve has two fitted numbers: a half-activation tension and a slope factor.
scenes.visual: On screen: P(open) = 1 / [1 + exp((T50 − T)/k)]. An S-shaped curve with T50 and k marked. Tag: assumes normalized current tracks fraction open.
scenes.narration: For a two-state channel at equilibrium, this gives the fraction of channels open. Patch papers fit the same curve to current. That reading assumes current tracks the fraction open. The curve has two fitted numbers: a half-activation tension and a slope factor.

scenes.tts: Match the two forms, and each number gets a meaning. The half-activation tension is the resting preference for closed, divided by the area gained.
scenes.visual: On screen: T50 = ΔG₀ / ΔA. The T50 mark on the curve is linked by an arrow to ΔG₀ and ΔA in the equation.
scenes.narration: Match the two forms, and each number gets a meaning. The half-activation tension is the resting preference for closed, divided by the area gained.

scenes.tts: The slope factor is thermal energy, divided by the area gained. More area means a smaller slope factor, and a steeper switch.
scenes.visual: On screen: k = k_B·T_abs / ΔA. As ΔA grows on a slider, the curve steepens.
scenes.narration: The slope factor is thermal energy, divided by the area gained. More area means a smaller slope factor, and a steeper switch.

scenes.tts: One unit note. Piconewtons per nanometre and millinewtons per metre are the same quantity.
scenes.visual: Unit card: 1 pN/nm = 1 mN/m. Labels: structural papers, patch papers.
scenes.narration: One unit note. Piconewtons per nanometre and millinewtons per metre are the same quantity.

scenes.tts: That is the one idea. Tension pays for area. In a two-state model, the area sets the steepness.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: Tension pays for area. Two-state model: T50 = ΔG₀/ΔA, k = k_B·T_abs/ΔA. Small note: k_B is Boltzmann's constant; T_abs is absolute temperature, not the tension T.
scenes.narration: That is the one idea. Tension pays for area. In a two-state model, the area sets the steepness.
